match.reason: The closest bank point, Entrepreneurship and innovation, covers entrepreneurs and innovation but not the full set of opportunity sources in the brief (market gaps, changing customer needs, R&D, new technology, global markets), so it is only a partial match and a new point is the safer choice.

draft.title: Sources of business opportunity
card: A business opportunity is a chance to meet a need and earn a return. It can come from several places.
a need that no business is meeting well, such as a suburb with no gluten-free bakery.
tastes, incomes, ages and habits shift over time, so buyers want new things. An ageing population creates demand for home care services.

a new tool can make new products or cheaper ways to work. Businesses also find opportunities in global markets, by selling to buyers overseas, and in research and development (R&D), which is work done to create new products or improve old ones.
draft.remember: Opportunities come from unmet needs, shifting customers, new ideas and tools, and new places to sell.

a.q: Ava notices that no business in her town sells fresh pasta, though many residents ask for it. What source of opportunity is this?
a.why: Customers want fresh pasta and no business supplies it, so there is an unmet need. That is a gap in the market. It is not R&D, because Ava has not tested or developed anything new.
a.clue: Is anyone in the town already meeting this need?

b.q: Over ten years, more Victorians work from home. Liam starts a business selling compact desks and ergonomic chairs for small flats. Which source of opportunity did he mainly act on?
opts: A gap caused by a new technology
b.why: Customers' work habits changed, so they wanted different products. That is changing customer needs. Liam did not sell overseas or run R&D, and he did not use any new technology to make his products.
b.clue: What changed about the customers themselves?

problems.detail: Global markets and R&D are tucked into the 'New technology' bullet. Students may read R&D and overseas selling as kinds of new technology rather than separate sources of opportunity.

The remember line sorts the sources into four neat groups, with 'new places to sell' as its own category. The card does not split them this way: it buries global markets inside the new technology bullet.

The distractor 'A gap caused by a new technology' is partly defensible. The rise in working from home was largely enabled by technology such as video calls and cloud tools. 'Mainly' keeps changing customer needs as the best answer, but the distractor could confuse careful students.

proposal.title: Sources of business opportunity
card: A business opportunity is a chance to meet a need and earn a profit. Common sources include innovation, gaps in the market, changing customer needs, R&D, new technology and global markets.

A gap in the market is a need no business is meeting well, such as a suburb with no gluten-free bakery. Changing customer needs arise as tastes, ages and habits shift, such as an ageing population wanting home care.

Research and development (R&D) is work a business does to create new products or improve old ones. New technology is a new tool, such as an app or machine, that makes new products or cheaper methods possible.
Global markets are buyers in other countries. Selling overseas can give a business far more customers than it could reach in Australia alone.
proposal.remember: Opportunities can come from unmet needs, shifting customers, R&D, new technology and overseas buyers.

a.q: Ava notices that no business in her town sells fresh pasta, though many residents ask for it. What source of opportunity is this?
a.why: Customers want fresh pasta and no business supplies it, so there is an unmet need. That is a gap in the market. It is not R&D, because Ava has not developed or improved any product.
a.clue: Is anyone in the town already meeting this need?

b.q: Over ten years, more shoppers in Geelong choose plant-based food for their health. Liam opens a deli stocking plant-based meals from local suppliers. Which source of opportunity did he act on?
b.why: Shoppers' tastes shifted over time, so they now want different food. That is changing customer needs. It is not R&D, because Liam sells meals that suppliers already make rather than developing new products himself.
b.clue: What changed about the shoppers themselves?
